scope: Reviewed authored English directions only. No student data.

records.text: Control the assembled hand. In this guide. An Ardweeno program reads three knobs and four buttons, then sends position numbers to five servo motors. A servo is a motor that moves toward a chosen position. Find the three knobs and four buttons on the assembled model. Keep the model disconnected while writing code. Check. You can point to all seven controls. Keep the existing wiring.

Open your team sketch. Ardweeno I D E > File. A sketch is an Ardweeno program. Work in one saved team copy so teammates do not replace each other’s changes. Open Ardweeno I D E. Open the latest numbered team sketch. For a first session, choose New Sketch and Save As RoboticHand_01. Check. You have one editable sketch with a numbered name.

Keep two empty sections. In the sketch editor. setup() runs once when the board starts. loop() repeats while the board runs. Curly braces mark the start and end of each section. For a new sketch, keep the two empty sections shown below. When continuing, find these sections in your existing code instead of adding duplicates. Check. There is one setup() and one loop(). Both have an opening { and a closing }.

Name the five servo motors. At the very top, before setup(). Servo.h supplies the motor instructions. Each Servo name is a separate box for one motor’s commands. Add the include line and five Servo names above setup(), outside both sections. Check. The sketch has five motor names, motor1 through motor5.

Name the buttons and starting values. Below the five Servo lines, before setup(). const int gives a fixed pin number a name. int stores a number that can change. The two button-controlled motors remember their last commands. Add these six lines below the Servo names and above setup(). Check. S1–S4 name pins 2–5. middleAngle starts at 125 and baseAngle at 86.

Match motors to signal pins. Inside setup(), between its braces. attach() tells the library which signal pin sends instructions to each motor. It can start servo signals when the program runs. Add the five attach lines. Check. Motor 1 uses D6, motor 2 D7, motor 3 D8, motor 4 D9 and motor 5 D10.

Prepare the buttons and starting commands. Inside setup(), after the attach lines. input pull up makes an unpressed button read high and a pressed button read low with the checked wiring. write() sends a position command to a motor. Add these lines inside setup(), after the five attach lines and before its closing brace. Check. All four buttons use input pull up. Motor4 starts with middleAngle and motor5 with baseAngle.

Check the setup code. Ardweeno I D E > Verify, the checkmark button. Verify checks whether the computer can compile your sketch. Compile means translating code into instructions the board can run. Verify does not run the hand. Ask the teacher to confirm the board type in the I D E, then choose Verify (the checkmark) with the model disconnected. Check. The I D E finishes without a compilation error.

Make knob one control motor one. At the start of loop(), inside its existing braces. Read, scale, send: analogRead gets a knob number from 0 to 1023. map changes that range to 0–57. write sends the new command to motor1. Add these three lines in order. Check. A one supplies pot1, angle1 holds the scaled value, and motor1 receives angle1.

Repeat the pattern for knobs two and three. Inside loop(), after the three knob-one lines. Each knob uses read, scale, send. Change the names, input pin and output range so it controls its own motor. Add these two three-line groups after knob one, inside loop(). Check. A two controls motor2 with 0–180 commands. A three controls motor3 with 0–90 commands.

Add the middle-up button. Inside loop(), after the knobs. if checks a condition. digitalRead(S3) == low means S3 is pressed. ++ adds one to middleAngle; the inner if caps it at 160 before write sends it. Add this complete S3 block. Check. Holding S3 raises middleAngle toward 160. It cannot keep increasing above 160 in this block.

Add the middle-down button. Inside loop(), after the complete S3 block. -- subtracts one. The lower limit check sets the command back to 90 if it went below 90. Add this complete S1 block. Check. Holding S1 lowers the motor4 command toward 90.

Add the base-up button. Inside loop(), after the complete S1 block. The base has its own remembered command, baseAngle. S4 adds one and stops the command at 176. Add the S4 block. Check. S4 commands motor5 toward 176.

Add the base-down button. Inside loop(), after the complete S4 block. S2 subtracts one from the base command. The lower limit keeps it at or above zero. Add the S2 block. Check. S2 commands motor5 toward 0.

Finish and verify the full program. At the end of loop(), then Ardweeno I D E > Verify. A short pause ends each pass through loop(). Verify checks whether the complete code can be translated for the selected board. Add delay(15); after the complete S2 block, before loop() closes. Choose Verify and save the numbered sketch when it passes. Check. One setup(), one loop(), all four button blocks and every limit check compile without errors.

Ask for the hardware check. At the assembled model, with the teacher. Servo signals can move the mechanism as soon as an uploaded program starts. Code numbers alone cannot establish safe physical movement. Show the teacher the saved code and ask them to check the real board, power, starting positions and allowed movement before connecting and uploading. Check. The teacher has checked the exact saved program, board, power and allowed movement. If the check is unavailable, leave hardware tests unrun.

Upload with the teacher. Ardweeno I D E board and port selection, with the teacher. Upload sends your program to the board. The hand can move as soon as setup() starts. After the hardware check, select the board and port the teacher identifies. Choose Upload with the teacher. Check. The I D E reports that uploading finished.

Test and record the three knobs. At the checked model, with the teacher. Testing one input at a time shows which input caused the response. A correct compile cannot tell us which physical part moved. Turn knob 1 slowly within the checked range and watch motor1. Repeat separately for knobs 2 and 3. Record each actual response under Test and improvement in the team report. Check. For each knob, your note names the sketch version, expected motor, actual movement and any problem.

Test and record the four buttons. At the checked model, with the teacher. Each button should change one remembered command in one direction while it is held. Releasing it stops that button block from changing the command. Try S1, S2, S3 and S4 separately within the checked range. Release each before trying the next. Add each actual response to the same test note. Check. S1/S3 command motor4 in opposite directions; S2/S4 command motor5 in opposite directions. Your notes say what actually moved.

Check one problem and retest. Ardweeno I D E and the test note, with the teacher. Changing one thing lets you see whether that change helped. If a control failed, compare its input, motor name and limits with the reference. After a teacher-checked correction, Verify, save a new numbered version and repeat that control test with teacher approval. Check. Your test note keeps the old result and the new result for the same control.

Explain the code in your team report. In your existing team report, under Project. Following one input through the code shows how the program produces an output. Under Project, explain one knob or button: input, value change, limit and motor. Keep the report headings Project; Research; Test and improvement; References. Check. Your explanation matches your saved code and test notes. A command limit is not a measured physical angle.

Save and share the tested version. Your computer file manager and existing team Drive folder. The next editor needs the real code and a clear note about what was checked. Save the sketch. Compress its whole numbered folder as a ZIP and upload it to the team folder. Check that it contains the matching .ino. Tell the next editor the filename and whether hardware tests ran. Check. The team has the latest editable program, its ZIP and the matching report. Earlier versions remain available.
